items.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI is often understood as an output-centered system that produces answers, drafts, plans, or recommendations. This paper argues that this view is useful but incomplete. In sustained, inquiry-led interaction, generative AI can also shape whether possibilities persist, develop, branch, shift direction, or close. The paper introduces AI as a Generative Pathway System, a conceptual model of pathway formation built around two mechanisms: Premature Closure Reduction and Continuation Scaffolding. Rather than treating continuation as inherently beneficial, the model positions Relational Integrity and Human Agency as governing conditions for responsible continuation. Drawing on path dependence, cognitive load theory, scaffolding, choice architecture, exploration–exploitation dynamics, and research on human–AI interaction, the paper develops a conceptual framework for examining how generative AI shapes the survival, direction, and governance of possibilities over time across individual, institutional, and collective contexts. The model’s central claim is that responsible pathway formation depends on mechanisms for opening and extending possibilities together with governing conditions that guide judgments about when continuation should be sustained, redirected, or responsibly discontinued.</jats:p>
title: AI as a Generative Pathway System: How Generative AI Reshapes Possibility, Continuation, and Human Agency

<jats:p>Most contemporary AI systems are evaluated as model snapshots or replaceable services: a better model appears, the old one is replaced, and success is measured primarily through immediate task performance. NEO (Neural Engine Operating System) begins from a different question: can an AI persist as the same developing entity across time, accumulate a life history, make mistakes, be corrected, change because of those experiences, and carry the resulting history forward even when its cognition engine changes? NEO is therefore not designed to maximize short-term benchmark performance. Its primary research object is developmental continuity. The architecture places a Persistent Entity lifecycle above a replaceable cognition engine and integrates verbatim life-history memory, source-authority-aware context projection, provisional Native Learning V2, usergoverned durable adaptation, a Canonical/FAST execution split, Self-Signal for governed self-initiation, Browser/World observation, and evidence-based Self-Diagnosis. The paper reports implementation and host-observed evidence from a consumer-PC deployment while distinguishing such evidence from long-term proof. It also argues that path-dependent divergence is not necessarily a defect: two NEO instances beginning from the same cognition engine may become meaningfully different if their life histories differ. The strongest current claim is architectural and developmental, not competitive: NEO demonstrates a working structure in which experience, error, correction, learning, governance, self-state, world observation, diagnosis, and resource control can belong to one continuing AI entity. Long-horizon development, largescale learning accumulation, and cross-engine Re-embodiment remain unproven and are currently constrained by available compute.

</div></jats:p>
title: NEO (Neural Engine Operating System): A Persistent Developmental AI Operating System — From Replaceable Cognition Models to a Life-History-Based AI Entity

items.abstract: <jats:p>The unprecedented acceleration of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and agentic ecosystems within United States organizations has outpaced established corporate risk management frameworks, creating a critical vulnerability vector. This study presents a systematic literature review analyzing the multi-tiered landscape of enterprise AI platform taxonomy, adoption dynamics, and cybersecurity risk classification. Evaluating an extensive body of retrieved records under a rigorous, multi-framework protocol compliant with PRISMA, Kitchenham, and Webster Watson standards, high-quality primary sources spanning peer-reviewed literature, international standards, and authoritative industry disclosures were synthesized. The review introduces five author-derived synthesis instruments: the Composite Adoption Score (CAS), the Enterprise AI Risk Classification Framework (EARCF), the Enterprise AI Platform Taxonomy (EAPT), the Enterprise AI Governance Maturity Model (EAGM), and the Enterprise AI Governance Lifecycle (EAGL). CAS and EARCF are proposed as comparative synthesis frameworks intended to support evidence classification and structured analysis rather than predictive assessment. Our findings show that generative AI adoption expanded rapidly across commercial segments, driven primarily by Tier-1 productivity suites and enterprise infrastructure APIs. Concurrently, the emergence of agentic architectures characterized by multi-step reasoning and autonomous tool-use capabilities has introduced acute vulnerabilities, including prompt injection, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) corpus poisoning, and excessive agency. Threat modeling demonstrates that while traditional security controls mitigate baseline boundary failures, they are less effective against autonomous state manipulation and memory-auditing lapses. Finally, by cross-mapping the coverage of dominant governance standards, including NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, OWASP LLM Top 10, and MITRE ATLAS, this review identifies significant gaps in multi-agent accountability protocols and memory-state auditing. The paper concludes by presenting a governance maturity roadmap designed to support the transition from ad hoc mitigation practices to auditable, zero-trust AI architectures.</jats:p>
title: Enterprise Generative AI: A Systematic Review of Security Risks and Governance

items.abstract: <jats:p>The lending field with blockchain-artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a significant transformation thanks to digital loans in governance apps, which provide quick, easy, and typically paperless transactions. There are several risks connected to the availability of data online, despite the fact that the entire loan process is simple and efficient. Because flash loans return to the same block of the Blockchain, which increases the likelihood that they will be tampered with, they are an important type of digital loan with AI that puts extra pressure on institutions to ensure security. The potential for predatory lending practices that target weaker payees must therefore be addressed. Consequently, this chapter has developed a security protocol based on the concept of cryptocurrency digital wallets with generative/explainable AI (GAI/XAI), which are protected by our use of the Xsalsa20 algorithm with blockchain. It has met the requirements and is enhanced by using the crocodile optimization algorithm (COA), which guarantees fast and efficient search results.</jats:p>
title: Blockchain and Generative/Explainable AI-Powered Wallet Cybersecurity to Protect Financial Procedures for the Funding System in Governance Apps

items.abstract: <jats:p>The fast-growing interconnection of digitized infrastructures and increasing sophistication of cyber-attacks have created unprecedented challenges for modern cybersecurity systems. Innovative technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI), Digital Twins, and Federated Learning offer new avenues for developing smart, adaptive, and resilient cybersecurity solutions, which can deal with the emerging threats. However, conventional cybersecurity systems are based on the use of centralized architecture, reactive approaches to threat detection, and static security concepts. Moreover, contemporary security solutions relying on artificial intelligence experience various limitations concerning the protection of personal information, threat intelligence sharing among organizations, and creating realistic cyber-attacks for simulation. Therefore, there is an acute need for designing a scalable and secure cybersecurity ecosystem that can predict potential threats and help implement autonomous defensive measures. It is crucial to address the existing limitations and create a solution capable of increasing cybersecurity resilience. This paper presents the development of the Federated Digital Twin-Based Cybersecurity Ecosystem Using Generative AI for Predictive Attack Simulation and Defense. This framework incorporates digital twin technology in order to model the changing cyber-environment, utilizes federated learning to facilitate distributed threat intelligence sharing and employs Generative AI for effective attack simulation and defense generation.</jats:p>
title: Predictive Cyber Security Ecosystem Based on Federated Digital Twins Using Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI).

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of Agentic Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its transformative impact on U.S. national security and defense operations. Agentic GenAI, characterized by autonomous systems capable of independent decision-making with minimal human intervention, represents a paradigm shift in military planning, cybersecurity, intelligence analysis, and logistics optimization. We examine the strategic imperatives driving Department of Defense initiatives, including recent partnerships with leading AI companies and substantial investments exceeding $800 million in frontier AI technologies. The study systematically evaluates the current ecosystem of development tools and frameworks-from commercial platforms like OpenAI Government and Scale AI's Thunderforge to specialized defense systems such as Virtualitics GenAI toolkit and C3 AI Enterprise Suite-while addressing critical security considerations through OWASP frameworks and verification methodologies. The paper also explores the role of verification frameworks like Independent Verification and Validation (IVV), intelligence tools such as Maltego, and development environments like Xcode in ensuring the reliability and security of agentic AI systems. Our analysis identifies key implementation challenges including technical reliability in contested environments, ethical concerns regarding autonomous decision-making, and organizational barriers to adoption. The paper proposes a detailed five-year roadmap (2024-2029) projecting the evolution from current foundational efforts to future strategic dominance, with parallel development of policy frameworks for responsible deployment. Through synthesis of recent defense publications, industry reports, and academic research, we provide actionable recommendations for human oversight standards, testing certification processes, workforce training, international governance, and incident response protocols.</jats:p>
title: Agentic Generative AI in U.S. National Security and Defense: Tools, Frameworks, and Policy Recommendations

items.abstract: <jats:p>Cloud deployment and usage span a wide range, from personal services to missioncritical enterprise resources. Such services and infrastructures are frequently used to support the generation of AI products, the risks of which often remain unassessed. Generative AI presents a rapidly evolving threat landscape , with novel impact and techniques valid for days, if not hours. Smaller operating teams and infrastructure managed by multiple partners increase the risks from accidents and misconfigurations. The advantages of generative AI include automation of mundane tasks, enabling detection of anomalous usage patterns, supporting incident detection and response, and facilitating generative security by developing automated defence mechanisms. However, these same advantages may be misused by attackers. Defence-in-depth architectures, with multiple overlapping controls, are a fundamental principle of security, but their implementation often reflects a legacy of compliance rather than risk management. Generative AI may assist with model and data governance and support risk-based hardening for public cloud services and third-party supply chains, yet these opportunities also remain largely unexplored. Given the conflicting pressures on operation teams, the full potential of generative AI cannot be exploited with manual deployment, and integrating generative AI capabilities will help organisations to achieve much closer to fully autonomous operations, greatly improving reliability and reducing resource requirements by concentrating human effort on exceptions.</jats:p>
title: Adaptive and Autonomous Security Frameworks Using Generative AI for Cloud Ecosystems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large-scale, interconnected power systems are susceptible to blackouts, which can result in significant financial losses, production cycle disruptions, and equipment damage at power plants. A forced islanding plan with an appropriate restoration process will work well to prevent these blackouts. This paper proposes a mechanism that divides the system into predetermined islands and determines the risk during an outage. In the event that there are unstable islands, an under-voltage load shedding plan is implemented to restore system stability. Furthermore, a restoration protocol has been developed. The suggested work is done using a six bus system as an example. This strategy can also be used in smart grid settings to raise the dependability and efficiency of the electricity system.</jats:p>

<jats:p>With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence and the sophistication of the digital environment, cybercrime is becoming more diverse and sophisticated, evolving into deepfakes, ransomware, phishing, virtual asset crimes, and dark web-based crimes. Accordingly, there are limitations to effectively preventing and responding to cybercrime through traditional, people-centered crime information analysis alone, and the need for an AI-based information analysis system that can quickly collect and analyze risk information at the stage before a crime occurs is increasing.
The purpose of this study is to present an AI-based cybercrime information analysis system and to propose its potential applications and development directions in the field of private security. To this end, the study focused on literature review and case analysis both domestically and internationally, comparing and analyzing AI-based cybercrime response systems in the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union (EU), and South Korea. It also reviewed key intelligence analysis technologies such as open-source intelligence (OSINT), natural language processing (NLP), machine learning, deep learning, and Generative AI, and proposed a model and operational system for building an AI intelligence analysis center applicable to the private security sector based on these technologies.
The results showed that AI-based information analysis improves the speed of data collection and the accuracy of analysis compared with conventional methods, and has high potential for use in crime prediction, abnormal behavior detection, internal information leak detection, and intelligent video analysis. On the other hand, inadequate personal data protection, data bias, explainability (explainable AI), and insufficient accountability and legal grounds for automated decision-making were identified as major factors undermining the reliability of AI-based information analysis. Therefore, this study proposed key improvement measures including training AI information analysis professionals, establishing an AI information-sharing platform among the police, private security firms, and the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA), introducing explainable AI, building a privacy protection system based on Privacy by Design, and establishing guidelines for the use of AI in private security.
This study holds academic significance in that it systematically proposes a cybercrime information analysis model that integrates AI technology with private security science, and it has practical significance in providing policy-based foundational data for the future establishment of AI-based private security information analysis centers and the development of a police–private sector collaborative cybercrime response system.</jats:p>
title: A Study on AI-Based Information Analysis of Cybercrime: Focusing on the Generative AI and the Private Security Information Analysis System

items.abstract: <jats:p>The advent of Generative AI has triggered a paradigm shift across several domains, resulting in ground-breaking advances in text, picture, video, audio, and code production. However, this technical advancement has also increased cyber security intimidations, as hackers increasingly use Generative AI in their harmful actions. Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) and Huge words models (HWMs) are transforming businesses throughout the world. However, their enormous promise carries major hazards. It is critical to address the cyber security concerns related with Gen-AI. This aids organizations in comprehending the security implications of these technologies. This chapter will provide a complete Gen-AI security architecture and show how it may help us protect Gen-AI apps, models, and the whole Gen-AI ecosystem. This research attempts to define the many security vulnerabilities posed by Generative AI, identifying their manifestations across different application areas.</jats:p>
title: Generative AI-Driven Security Frameworks for Web Engineering
